items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1995-08-29
items.q: Ernie and I had kept a beautiful relationship all of our lives... Ernie and I were in high school together.

ctx.x: No, no, no. That's a faster train. Let's go back. Let's go back for a second. So you worked at JBW. No. JBW, no. What was your further first station you went?

Well, after that, now, here comes WMRY, which is now WYLD. That's wild. WMRY started in the French Quarter by the Court of Two Sisters. Ernie Branger, who was Ernie the whip, he was the major black disc jockey down there. Well, Ernie and I had kept a beautiful relationship all of our lives because he knew my children, I knew his children, I knew his wife and so forth. Even his oldest child today still calls me his uncle. Well, anyway, Ernie and I were in high school together. So, Ernie said, why don't you come to…
Is Israel Augustine the same? He was a DJ?

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-01-10
items.q: The interviewee mentions 'Ernie' in the context of radio programming: 'But even though rock and roll and Dr. Daddy or Ernie, they got more mail...'

ctx.x: Okay, so why don't we try to, okay, we're back with Tech Stevens, January 10th, 1996, reel number one. Okay. Yeah, let's try to get the microphones closer and you know how that stuff goes. Wait, so we're talking about, we're talking about advertising and stuff, that's okay, just advertising, not advertising, we're talking about, you brought up the Dawn Patrol, why don't you continue on who was the Dawn Patrol and what it was? Well, the Dawn Patrol was started

by the Pittsburgh Courier in order to enhance the musical structure in and around the greater metropolitan area of New Orleans that everything would start around about midnight. And for all of the bands who probably played at the French Quarter, or maybe some of the other clubs in and around the city, if you go on, like Club Desire, like the Robin Hood, maybe some who played just any place, maybe the Lloyd's at Square Lounge on the West Bank of the River, or maybe on Jesse's over in Marrero, or maybe at Louis…
All righty. You know, Ted, I think it's about time that we start talking about a young man who had one of the greatest radio trademarks ever in history.

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-01-10
items.q: they had Ernie the Whipple, myself, I think, Oka Dopa was in there. Well, they had a few of us in there.

ctx.x: Well, when you hear that terminology, what does that mean? You heard it in the mid-fifties. You first heard it.

Well, when I first heard it, I looked at it and said, rock and roll. Well, you see, Roy Brown, like I said, really started this thing in New Orleans, even before Fats Domino, in a sense, because he had this good rock and tonight thing, and he had this band with Bob Bob Ockton. Bob Ockton was an ordinary, but he was a drummer. He died a couple of years back, you know, and incidentally, some of his relatives say, no, I'm no real business right now. I talk to him every now and then. So, when you're good rocking…

Well, well, did you, I know you probably did, and there's a whole article in the Jazz Archivist. Yeah. And we're talking about New Orleans in the 60s, and they're talking about, a lot of it about the modern jazz scene. Did you follow the pop, the bebop scene in New Orleans?
